# Pipeline Babysitting

Manual pipeline watching should be rare. The default is automation: run it and let your monitoring catch the failure. The only exception is when you're actively debugging or making a decision that hinges on intermediate results—and even then, the goal is to gather enough information to hand off, not to stay pinned to your screen.

When you're allowed to step away depends entirely on what happens if the run fails silently. If a failed build is caught by CI before it can break main, by all means kick it off and move on. If a failed deployment silently leaves your service half-upgraded in an inconsistent state, you're watching it. If a data pipeline is running against production and a stale cache will silently corrupt tomorrow's numbers, same deal.

Before anyone says "I'll check back in ten minutes," verify three things. First: there's a notification channel (a Slack webhook, a dashboard alert, an email) that will fire immediately on failure—and someone is actually listening to it. If the alert goes to a channel no one reads until Monday, you're just lying about checking back in. Second: someone knows how to read the failure. A cryptic stack trace is not a notification; an oncall engineer who can triage it is. Third: there's a kill switch. If the run goes sideways, can you stop it before it's done any damage? Some runs are safe to let burn down; others aren't. If you wouldn't know what to do with a failure before it happens, you have to be there to prevent it.

The rule is simple: you can only walk away from a run if you've already walked away from it at least once and been wrong about what would happen. Anything else is guessing, and guessing costs everyone's afternoon.
